work.author: Severian of Gabala
work.title: In ascensionem domini nostri Iesu Christi et in principium Actorum

paragraphs.text: Our wealth, our treasure and the springs of eternal life are the Savior's saving dispensations. We thirst to speak of them and hasten to proclaim them, but we are not able to describe them worthily. Yet gripped by longing, mastered by its force and confessing our weakness, we take refuge, as in a calm harbor, in that prophetic saying: "Who shall tell of the mighty deeds of the Lord, or make all his praises heard?" Consider that great prophet himself, to whom God made known the unseen and hidden things of his wisdom: blessed David, who was counted worthy to be called the father of Christ, great among prophets, glorious among kings, the friend of God, whose heart God so honored that he himself said, "I have found David the son of Jesse, a man after my own heart." If even he, so great and so eminent, looked upon the greatness of the knowledge of God and said, "Your knowledge is too wonderful for me; it is mighty, I cannot attain to it"; if the prophet grows faint as he gazes on the greatness of God's power; if Paul too, the theologian and heavenly trumpet, cries out, "O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past tracing out!"; if the tongues of prophets and apostles poured out such streams that the whole earth was filled with the knowledge of the Lord, as abundant water covers the seas; if such great rivers, flowing together into a sea of godliness, confessed their defeat in order to show the power of the One they proclaimed — where will the tiny drop of our little word even be seen, when so vast a sea of wisdom lies before us? Still, we must not grow numb as we look at the greatness of theology. We must look to God's purpose and venture boldly on divine teaching. For God awards the prize not by the worth of what is said, but by the longing of those who preach and the love of those who listen. When affectionate fathers see their children lisping and stumbling over their words, they look not at the halting speech but at the longing that comes from nature, and the children's lisping is sweeter to them than all the grand eloquence of rhetoric and all the lofty speculation of philosophy. In the same way God looks not at our tongues as they lisp about theology, but at our longing and our disposition: that we preach in faith and sing his praises in love. For nothing can be spoken clearly by a human tongue; whatever we say about God, we say lisping. Why? Because Paul too cries out, "We know in part and we prophesy in part." Yet even though we lisp, he has entrusted to us the proclamation of peace. That is why Isaiah cries, "And the lisping tongues shall learn to speak peace." Come then, quietly and little by little, let us lisp to our common Father and Master, who was pleased to say to his own disciples, "Little children." If he calls us children, he puts up with his children's lisping.

He has already ascended into heaven, and his much-hymned ascension has been proclaimed. But grace is not shut out by time, nor is theology confined to particular days. We wished to go up to the Mount of Olives but were prevented, as Christ knows: we had planned to, but were hindered by the unsettled weather and the press of the crowd. I say this to remove every ground for suspicion from those who want to accuse us without cause. Then, seeing how much had already been said, we quickly cut our sermon short, so as not to bury your memory under a multitude of words. So today we pay the debt. After all, the law allowed someone who had not kept the Passover in the first month to pay that debt in the second month. You must understand that God's word is not confined to times or days. Every day it welcomes the proclamation of the cross, the passion, the resurrection, the ascension and the second coming.

First let us quietly go over a few of the divine words in today's reading and draw from the springs of the Gospel, and in this way come to what we promised. "When it was evening on that day, the first day of the week, and the doors were shut where the disciples were gathered, Jesus came." From the time the Savior accomplished the resurrection for us, he seldom appeared to the disciples on any day other than the Lord's day. Just as he used to go to the synagogue every Sabbath in order to fulfill the law, so, from the time he accomplished the resurrection and brought its pledge to the world, he made a point of appearing on the Lord's day, the first day of the week, to lay the foundation of the holy Lord's day. For the observance of the Sabbaths was coming to its end, and the observance of the Lord's day, that is, of the resurrection, was making its beginning, as you remember from what was said earlier. How does blessed Matthew put it, as he marks the close of the Sabbaths and introduces the beginning of the holy Lord's days? "Late on the Sabbaths." For this was the end, the late close of the first Sabbaths. "As it began to dawn toward the first day of the week." So he appeared after rising on the first day of the week, on the very day of the holy feast of the resurrection.

"The doors being shut where the disciples were gathered for fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood in the midst." Where fear is at its height, the One who dispels fear arrives. Where the storm is at its height, calm shines out. Where he sees the ship of godliness tossed by the storm, he brings his skill as a helmsman: he stills the storm and brings the ship into calm water, and so he brings the remedy for fear when that passion is at its height. "He stood in the midst." And what does he say? "Peace be with you." Let your mind not be in turmoil; let your reasoning not be troubled; do not be under attack from fearful thoughts. "Peace be with you." Peace abolishes war, dissolves fear and drives out enmity. "Peace be with you." God often gave peace to human beings, but not in the person of the Sovereign himself. He gave it through angels and through prophets. The Savior alone appeared in his own person and gave peace. Peace was given to Daniel, but through an angel. An angel appeared to Daniel and said, "Peace be with you, man greatly beloved; be strong and of good courage; the Lord is with you." An angel also appeared to Gideon and said, "Peace be with you." So angels gave peace, but the Master of the angels had not yet given it. He sent peace through them, but kept the peace of the Gospel stored up in himself. The prophets often received peace from angels, but they thirsted to receive it from the very person of the Sovereign. That is why Isaiah cried, "O Lord our God, give us peace": give us peace not through others but through yourself. Then comes the answer to that prayer: "My peace I give to you." "And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and his side." A general who returns from war shining with the wounds of victory is not ashamed of them, for they are more splendid than crowns. In the same way the Savior, who had taken wounds for the sake of the truth and of the whole human race, does not hide his sufferings but uncovers them, to show his courage. He showed the hands that bore the marks of the nails, and he showed his side as well: the hands with which he fashioned us, the side from which he made the fountain of the mysteries gush out for us. He showed his hands to give full assurance of the resurrection, to assure those who doubted that the One who suffered had truly risen, that the body which had died and been buried had truly been raised. 4. "Then the disciples were glad when they saw the Lord." Peace was given, fear was dispelled, grace blossomed. "So he said to them again, 'Peace be with you.'" Why again? When he wants to make the gifts of grace secure, he doubles his blessings, as with Abraham: "Blessing I will bless you, and multiplying I will multiply you." In the same way he gives peace upon peace to those who are near and to those who are far off.

"As the Father has sent me, so I send you." Pay attention, I beg you. See how he puts the saving dispensation in terms of his human condition. He did not say, "As the Father begot me," for the word "sending" points to his human condition. We keep stressing this because he is explaining the dispensation. Where the divine nature itself is spoken of plainly, he means, it proclaims Father and Son. "As he has sent me." But how did he send you? Pay attention, I beg you. You, Master, were sent from heaven, but the apostles are not from heaven. How then do you send them as the Father sent you? "When I say 'as he sent me,'" he answers, "I do not mean the manner of the sending, but its power. I was sent to suffer for the world. I send you so that through your sufferings I may crown the whole world." And since mortal nature was not able to attain to the likeness of the Master, the Gospel says, "And when he had said this, he breathed on them." What nature lacked, he supplied by grace: "And when he had said this, he breathed on them and said to them, 'Receive the Holy Spirit.'" Pay attention. Why did the Savior breathe on the apostles, and on the very day of the resurrection? Could he not have given the Holy Spirit without breathing on them? It is because, when he fashioned the first man, he breathed into his face, and the man became a living soul. But man lost the grace of that breath through his transgression, and having lost its life-giving power he was dissolved into dust, and in the grave the work of his making was undone. So now, renewing what he had fashioned and restoring the ancient gift, he breathed into the faces of the apostles, giving back to his creature that ancient, life-giving power. At the same time what the prophet had foretold was also fulfilled. The blessed prophet Nahum foresaw that the Savior, on rising from the dead, would breathe on the holy apostles and fill them with divine grace, and he solemnly charges the people: "Keep your feasts, O Judah; pay your vows to God; for they shall never again come to grow old. It is finished; it is taken away. For he has come up from the earth who breathes into your face and delivers you from affliction." He mentions both things, since the Lord both dispelled their fear and breathed on them, giving them the Spirit. He said, "He who breathes into your face and delivers you from affliction."

Then he says, "Peace be with you," and "when he had said this, he breathed on them and said to them, 'Receive the Holy Spirit.'" He saw human nature buckling under its labors and, through weakness, shrinking from the contest. So he fills up what was lacking with the power of the Spirit, to comfort our nature as it struggles in our weakness. Like iron, he tempered it with divine grace, so that what it does not have by nature it might receive from grace, and go out to the contest braced by the power of the Spirit. "Receive the Holy Spirit. As the Father has sent me, so I send you." "But you," they might say, "came forth as Master. You saw sinners and had mercy; you forgave our sins. Grace stands higher than we do. We keep falling into the abyss of sin. Sinners are many, and much loving-kindness is needed. We do not have the authority. How can we be sent as you were?" Therefore, so that the words "As the Father sent me, so I send you" might be fulfilled, he says, "If you forgive anyone's sins, they are forgiven; if you retain anyone's, they are retained." He gives the very authority he has. A ruler cannot be entrusted with a nation unless he receives power to pardon, to put to death and to punish. In the same way the Savior, about to appoint them rulers of the world, gives them power both to punish and to pardon: "If you forgive anyone's sins, they are forgiven; if you retain anyone's, they are retained." For no one can possibly bear witness nobly as a martyr, or preach earnestly, or achieve any great and difficult deed, unless the power of the Holy Spirit braces the witness's strength. Otherwise they cannot be witnesses. By a martyr, or witness, I now mean not only the one who is made perfect through suffering, but also the one who bears witness to grace by his word. For every herald of the truth is a witness of God. That is why the Gospel says of John the Baptist, "And John bore witness to the truth, saying, 'This is he.'" What makes a witness here is not suffering but crying out. It is impossible to become witnesses of the divine word without being braced by the Holy Spirit. That is why the Savior says as he is being taken up, "But stay in the city of Jerusalem until you are clothed with power from on high; and you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses." For without receiving the power of the Spirit it is impossible to become a witness.

"But Thomas, one of the twelve, called the Twin, was not with them." It was a very great dispensation of Christ that Thomas was left out, so that his doubt might prove the resurrection all the more forcefully. Suppose Thomas had not been left out and had not doubted because of it, and the Savior had not given full assurance to answer his doubt. Then the miracle of the resurrection would still have caused many to stumble. As it was, his doubt became the healing of all the faithful. "So when Thomas came, the other disciples said to him, 'We have seen the Lord.'" They took pride in what they had seen. He, for his part, was held by a kind of contrariness rather than by unbelief; it went no further than doubt. He thirsted for full assurance, and he did not say, "This cannot possibly have happened." Pay close attention. He did not deny the resurrection. He did not say, "You are talking about impossible things; you are reporting things that cannot happen." Instead he asked for full assurance, saying, "Unless I see in his hands the mark of the nails, and put my finger into the mark of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe." He did not say, "I will never believe at all," but, "Unless I am fully assured, I will not believe." "And after eight days." See how he comes on the next Lord's day, for from one Lord's day to the next is eight days. "And eight days after the resurrection Jesus came again, the doors being shut, and stood in the midst and said, 'Peace be with you.'" Since on the earlier occasion he said "Peace be with you" twice, here he said it once, so that he might make the gift of peace complete, from the Holy Trinity: "Peace be with you." Then he says to Thomas, "Bring your finger here." Pay attention, I beg you. The Savior does not wait to hear about Thomas's doubt from the disciples. He was not informed first and then began to teach. To convince Thomas that he had been present even when he could not be seen, and to examine his doubt himself, he says to Thomas, "Bring your finger here," as you said, "and see my hands; and bring your hand and put it into my side; and do not be unbelieving, but believing." He shows that someone who demands proof is not a believer, while someone who submits to faith is. Probing Christ's side and the marks of the nails is like asking, "How was he begotten?" Or rather, it is not like it at all. Thomas wanted to see the marks of nails, visible in flesh and perceptible to the senses. He wanted to see something that had actually happened, something he already knew about. But you pry into a nature that cannot be seen, an essence beyond comprehension, an ineffable begetting, a Begetter beyond words, a Begotten beyond comprehension. Are you not transgressing far worse? Are you not worse than an unbeliever? If blessed Thomas probed a side and was told, "Do not be unbelieving," then you who probe the incorporeal nature and the incomprehensible power must hear it too: "Do not be unbelieving, but believing." Still, we give thanks for God's forbearance, because Thomas's finger became a pen of godliness. It tore apart the nets of the heretics and stopped the mouths of those who dare to say that he put on a body only in appearance and died only in appearance. Thomas's finger dispelled the heretics' doubt as surely as that other finger did, the one the Egyptian magicians could not stand against, when they said, "This is the finger of God." Once he had received full assurance, it would have been fitting for holy Thomas to say David's words, "In the day of my affliction I sought God," and, since he had searched with his hands, to say what follows: "with my hands, by night, before him, and I was not deceived." "Do not be unbelieving, but believing."

From the marks Thomas saw the One who had suffered, and from his foreknowledge he recognized God, and so he says, "My Lord and my God." Let the heretics listen. If the Son truly declined such titles and is not equal in honor with the Father, why does he not refuse an honor that goes beyond him? On another occasion someone addressed him as "Good Teacher," and he says, "Why do you call me good? No one is good but God alone." And yet the word "good" is in common use even among us. If, as you suppose, he refused to be called good, should he not much more have refused to be called God and Lord? There he hears "Good Teacher" and says, "Why do you call me good?" Here he hears "My Lord and my God," and he did not say, "Why do you call me Lord and God?" There, the form of address was unworthy of him, for the man did not say "Good Lord" but "Good Teacher"; so he rejected the lesser title. Here he accepted the glorious one. There he found fault, and here too he found fault, but for the opposite reason: that Thomas spoke too late. He found fault with him not for saying "My Lord," but for saying it late. "Because you have seen, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen and have believed." One man was reproached, and all of us were blessed. This beatitude passes on to all of us and to those who come after us: we did not receive the miracles by sight but accept them by faith, and so we become sharers in this great and glorious blessing.

But now let us move on from the narrative, which we have run through briefly, to another prophetic saying, if you are not worn out by how much has been said already: "Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord." For the Savior was taken up from the Mount of Olives. "Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, and to the house of the God of Jacob." God has honored our city too by giving it a name like that of the mountain. There the Savior was taken up from the mountain called the Mount of Olives, and here, under the same name, the place called Elaia, "the Olive," has been planted, confirming the ancient story by its nearness and by its name. For the Savior led the disciples up to the Mount of Olives, and the Mount of Olives was opposite Jerusalem. So pay attention to that place and to this one. "Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord." Let us go up with him in longing and in word, and see what his saving ascension has accomplished for us.

I want, then, to trace the book of Acts itself, step by step from its opening words, so that I may draw the divine streams together with you, and we may search out its treasures in common, like merchants of the truth, eager to grow rich in godliness. "The Acts," it says, "of the Apostles." This title itself shows the whole force of what the book contains, and the opening serves as the announcement of the entire work. Not all the apostles' acts appear in the book. If you look carefully, the first part of the book sets out the miracles and teaching of Peter, with only a little about the other apostles; after that the whole work is given over to Paul. Peter is mentioned, and Paul; how then are these the acts of all the apostles? Blessed Paul says that when one member is honored, all the members share in its honor. So the historian did not title it "The Acts of Peter and Paul" but "of the Apostles." The praise is shared by all, and so is the announcement.

So we ask who composed this book of the Acts. Many people have split into many different opinions on this. Some say that Clement of Rome composed it, others say Barnabas, and others Luke the evangelist. Since their reasoning divides into different opinions, let us take the writer himself as our interpreter: who he is, what he is doing, and whether he points the account to himself. He says: "In the first book, O Theophilus, I gave an account of all things." By saying "first," he sends our minds to ask which first book he means. If this were the only one he had composed, he would not have said, "The first I made." So this book turns out to be the second, for "the first I have already made." And he himself tells us which first book he made: "In the first book, O Theophilus, I gave an account of all that Jesus began to do and to teach." In the first book he composed not Acts but a Gospel: not what Peter and Paul did, but what Jesus began to do and to teach. It is clear, then, that Luke, who composed the Gospel, also put together the Acts. But pay attention, and let us see whether it really is he. "In the first book, O Theophilus, I gave an account of all that Jesus began to do and to teach, until the day when he was taken up, after he had given commands through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he had chosen." That is: "I told the deeds and the teachings of the Savior up to the ascension." Pay attention, I beg you. "My first work," he says, "contains the works and teachings of the Lord, and my first book reached as far as the ascension." Now you find that neither Matthew at all, nor Mark except in part, nor John carried the Gospel through to the ascension, but only Luke. For Matthew ends his Gospel like this: "The eleven disciples went to the mountain in Galilee where Jesus had directed them. And he appeared to them, and they worshiped him; and he said, 'Go and make disciples of all nations. And behold, I am with you until the end of the age.'" That is the end of the Gospel, and he did not say how Jesus was taken up. Mark likewise says: "And the women went out from the tomb and said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid." After other things he speaks of the ascension briefly, like this: "So the Lord, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God. And they went out and preached everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the word through the signs that accompanied it. Amen." That is the end of the Gospel. Mark gives no extended account of the ascension. John told of the Savior's appearance at the Lake of Tiberias, when he says to Peter, "Peter, do you love me?", and completed that conversation. But then John left off and made no mention of the ascension. Instead he says: "Jesus did many other signs as well; if they were written down one by one, I suppose that the world itself could not contain the books that would be written." So John did not mention the ascension at all, nor did Matthew, and Mark did not mention it at length. Luke, however, carried his account right through to the ascension. That is why he says: "In the first book, O Theophilus, I gave an account of all that Jesus began to do and to teach, until the day when he was taken up, after he had given commands to the apostles whom he had chosen."

Who is this Theophilus? In those times he was a governor. While he held office he received the preaching; he received it while in office. The proconsul of Cyprus once received Paul's preaching while he was actually serving as proconsul, and in the same way Theophilus, who was a governor at the time, received the preaching through Luke. He then asks the blessed Luke to compose the Acts of the Apostles for him as well. "You taught me the works of the Savior," he says; "teach me also the works of the disciples." That is why Luke addresses the second book to him, for the Gospel according to Luke was also written to Theophilus. How is this clear? Luke himself says: "Since many have undertaken to set down an account of the events that have been fulfilled among us, just as they were handed down to us by those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and servants of the word, it seemed good to me also, having followed all things closely from the first, to write them for you in order, most excellent Theophilus, so that you may know the certainty of the things in which you have been instructed." "Most excellent" means "most illustrious," for at that time the title "most excellent" was given to the most illustrious. How is this clear? Festus the governor says to Paul, "You are mad, Paul," and Paul says to the governor, "I am not mad, most excellent Festus." So too here: "Most excellent Theophilus." Having told the Gospel and addressed it to Theophilus, then, he addresses this book to the same man.

"In the first book, O Theophilus, I gave an account of all that Jesus began to do and to teach." And how far did you carry your account? "Until the day when he was taken up, after giving commands to the holy apostles whom he had chosen through the Holy Spirit." The word order is transposed. It means: "I composed the Gospel up to the day when he was taken up, after he had given instructions to the apostles whom he had chosen." Pay attention, I beg you. "To them he also presented himself alive after his suffering." See the evangelist's boldness: even in the Acts he does not leave off theology. He did not say "to whom he showed himself," but "to whom he presented himself alive." For he says, "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." "To them he also presented himself alive after his suffering, by many proofs, appearing to them over forty days and speaking about the kingdom of God." The ascension was in fact the day before yesterday, since forty days are completed from the resurrection to the ascension. For at Pentecost there was not the ascension but the coming of the Holy Spirit.

Pay attention, I beg you. "By many proofs, appearing to them over forty days and speaking about the kingdom of God." He did not appear to them on each of the forty days. For after the resurrection he invested his flesh with great dignity, so that seeing him continually would not weaken the greatness of his power. Having risen, he had from then on to appear in divine forms, not through the familiarity of plain sight. That is why it says, "by many proofs over forty days." It was not plain sight but proofs that it was he, for he appeared with a different voice, a different form, a different appearance. He often came to the apostles and was not recognized. He came to Peter and his companions while they were fishing and said, "Children, do you have any fish?" And they did not recognize him, neither his form nor his voice. Then he says, "Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some"; and when they cast it, they caught many. Since they had not recognized him by sight, they recognized him from the proofs of his power. That is why the evangelist John says to Peter, "It is the Lord." He was convinced not by sight but by the proof of power. That is why Luke cries out: "By many proofs, appearing to them over forty days and speaking."

Not simply "appearing," but appearing at particular times. If we look closely, we find that he appeared eleven times to the holy apostles, and then was taken up. He had eleven disciples, since Judas had been cast out and had lost his own place and rank through the wicked betrayal he committed. So he appears to the apostles eleven times, not to all of them together but in different ways, now to some, now to others. For example, when he appeared to the ten, Thomas was not present; then he appeared again with Thomas present. Let us examine the number and see how it adds up, if he appeared eleven times because of the eleven apostles. First he appeared to Mary at the tomb and to the other women. The women saw him before anyone else; the blessed Isaiah also summons them: "Women coming from the sight, come and tell us." So he appeared to the women. Whoever wants to keep an exact count, let him watch that we do not miscount anywhere. First, to the women, Mary and the other women; then to Peter; then to Cleopas and his companion on the road, when they were going to Emmaus, when he was made known in the breaking of the bread. How is it clear, you ask, that he was seen by Peter before these two? Cleopas and his companion came in that evening to report to the disciples, "We have seen the Lord." And they found the apostles saying, "The Lord has truly risen and has appeared to Simon." While the two were reporting what they had seen, the news had already got ahead of them that Peter had seen the Lord. Paul also indicates this when he says: "For I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received, that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, and that he rose and appeared to Cephas, then to the eleven." First to Peter, then to the others. So he appeared to the women; then to Peter; then to Cleopas and his companion; then to the ten, without Thomas; then to the eleven, with Thomas present. That makes five. Then he appears again to five hundred brethren, for Paul indicates this too when he says: "Then he appeared to more than five hundred brethren at once, most of whom remain until now." That makes six. Then to the seven at the Sea of Tiberias; then, according to Paul, he appeared to James; then to all the apostles. Paul is not speaking of the eleven here, for he had already said, "he appeared to Cephas, then to the eleven." Then he appeared to the seventy, that is, "to all the apostles." Pay attention, I beg you. So you have, first, the women; Peter; Cleopas and his companion; the appearance to the ten, without Thomas; to the eleven, with Thomas present; the appearance to the five hundred, which makes six; seventh, to the seven; eighth, to James; ninth, to the seventy; tenth, on the mountain in Galilee; eleventh, on the Mount of Olives. Since at his ascension the Savior repeated "peace" many times, it would be wrong for us not to repeat the count to confirm it. So you have: first, the women; second, Peter; third, Cleopas and his companion; fourth, the ten; fifth, the eleven; sixth, the five hundred; seventh, the seven; eighth, James; ninth, the seventy; tenth, on the mountain in Galilee; eleventh, on the Mount of Olives.

"Appearing to them over forty days and speaking about the kingdom of God. And while he was eating with them, he ordered them not to leave Jerusalem, but to wait for the promise of the Father." Oh, the great forbearance of the Savior! Oh, his great goodness! Granted, Master, before the passion you ate and reclined at table with the disciples. Why do you eat with them after the resurrection? "So that I may confirm in them the wonder of the resurrection," he says. Even though this happened, there are some who still disbelieve the resurrection even now. If it had not happened, and he had not eaten and drunk with them, who could have persuaded those unbridled mouths, which so readily dare to say anything at all about the Savior's dispensation?

From this we are taught to honor the divine and mystical table. Often what speech could not accomplish, a table has accomplished. Often countless counselors could not resolve a single enmity, and one table has put an end to wars. Take the proof from the principal case. We never stopped being enemies of God, at war with the divine word, as Paul says: "While we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son." We were enemies. The law was sent, and it did not reconcile us. Prophets came, and they did not persuade us. God's enemies remained enemies and foes. There were many tyrants against the truth, many who fought God against piety, many words, many teachings, and they did not end the war. Christ came. He set up his own table, set himself out as food, and said, "Take, eat." At once he ended the war and awarded peace. In Egypt he scourges those who fight God, and no one obeys; he strikes the tyrants, and no one is persuaded. Here he sets himself out as food, and all eat. Scourging did not persuade them; being eaten, he persuades. I say "being eaten" with reference to the mystical table. "For I," he says, "am the bread that came down from heaven and gives life to the world."

"And while eating with them he spoke about the kingdom of God; and he ordered them not to leave Jerusalem, but to wait for the promise of the Father, which you heard from me." Granted, we heard it from you, for you said, "I am going up to my Father, and I will ask, and I will send you the Spirit of truth, the Paraclete." You said it. But when did the Father promise? He did not say, "wait for my promise," but "the promise of the Father, which you heard from me." The Father promised; I reminded you. And where did he promise? Unroll the whole Gospel and you will not find the voice of the Father promising to give the Holy Spirit to the disciples. So where did he promise? In the prophets, as Paul says: "Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God, which he promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures concerning his Son." So having promised the Gospel beforehand, he also promised beforehand to give the Holy Spirit. Where, then, is the promise? I am searching with you as one of you, one of you in faith and in love for Christ. I have often told your charity that sheep and shepherds are a human distinction, but in relation to Christ all are sheep. For both those who shepherd and those who are shepherded are shepherded by the one Shepherd above. So where did he promise? God says through the prophet Joel: "In the last days, says the Lord Almighty, I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh, and your sons and your daughters will prophesy." There is the promise. And where is its fulfillment? When the Holy Spirit came upon the apostles and gave them the diversity of tongues, and they spoke in tongues. People suspected they were drunk, and Peter says: "Men of Israel, why do you take these men to be drunk? It is only the third hour of the day. But this is what was spoken by the prophet Joel: 'In the last days, says the Lord, I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh.'" This is the promise of the Father.

But how is it clear that the promise was spoken in the person of the Father? I know that the Son also speaks in the prophets, so how do we know it was the Father speaking? "I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh, and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. And I will give signs in the heaven above and on the earth below, blood and fire and vapor of smoke." I have often said that the blood is the blood from his side, for it was a sign to see blood coming from a dead body. The blood is that from his side; the fire is the fire upon the apostles. "Blood and fire and vapor of smoke. The sun will be turned to darkness and the moon to blood, before the great and manifest day of the Lord comes." See how God the Father, who is speaking, refers to the Son when he says, "before the day of the Lord comes." He does not say, "my day." If you are the one giving the signs, how do you shift the meaning to another by saying, "before the great and manifest day of the Lord comes"? Pay attention. Perhaps someone will say that the prophet is speaking in his own person when he says, "before the day comes." But the prophet could not say, "I will pour out my Spirit, before the great and manifest day of the Lord comes. And everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved." This, then, is what God says in the prophets. And Paul follows it up, saying: "The same Lord is Lord of all, rich toward all who call on him. For everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved." Then, to show that this was said of Christ, he says: "How then will they call on him in whom they have not believed? And how will they believe in him of whom they have not heard? And how will they hear without someone preaching? And how will they preach unless they are sent? As it is written: How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news of good things, who bring good news of peace!"

Pay attention, I beg you. "He ordered them," it says, "not to leave Jerusalem, but to wait for the promise of the Father, which you heard from me: that John baptized with water, but you will be baptized in the Holy Spirit not many days from now." After the forty days there were ten days until Pentecost, on which the Holy Spirit appeared and baptized the apostles, not with water but with fire. This resolves the question that many people raise. Many have asked whether the apostles had been baptized with the baptism of the Gospel before the Savior's passion. For our part, we neither make our own pronouncements nor entrust so weighty a case to human reasoning; we follow what is written. We find that the apostles received a baptism before Christ's passion: the baptism of John the Baptist. Before the passion the Savior does not give another baptism. He does not want to undo John's preaching and give the Jews who opposed him a pretext to say that he had brought in another baptism of his own to insult John the Baptist. Instead he lets them keep the pledge of the water, while reserving the grace of the Spirit for them. That is why he speaks to them as to men who had not yet received the Spirit: "Receive the Holy Spirit." And after the resurrection he says: "Go to Jerusalem and wait for the promise of the Father, which you heard from me: that John baptized with water, but you will be baptized in the Holy Spirit not many days from now." No longer with water, for they had received that, but with the Holy Spirit. He does not add water to water, but supplies what was lacking to what fell short.

"But you will be baptized in the Holy Spirit not many days from now," that is, after ten. What need was there for the interval, then? What need, I mean, for the ten days in between? He was training the apostles' faith. While grace stayed quiet and nothing appeared, their faith was being trained, to see whether they would wait for the one who had promised, as one who does not lie. He promised and said, "Not many days from now." He did not specify the number of days; he said only, "not many days from now." He does not let us know everything, but he shows that the Master's ordering has its own measures. What you hear, learn; what you are not taught, do not pry into.

"But you will be baptized in the Holy Spirit." So when the Holy Spirit came upon them on the day of Pentecost, it filled the whole house where they were, so that they would be baptized in the Spirit as if in water. And together with the invisible sight he joined the visible one, the sight of the tongues. So they were baptized in the Spirit. Another narrative bears witness that this very baptism was the receiving of the Holy Spirit. The disciples accused Peter: "Why did you go in to Greeks and instruct them, and give them a share in baptism and the mysteries?" He says: "I was in the city of Joppa, and a certain centurion, Cornelius, sent for me. I went and taught the word, and as I was speaking, the Holy Spirit fell upon them, just as it did on us at the beginning." And to show that the coming of the Spirit on Cornelius and his household was a baptism, Peter at once says: "I remembered the word of the Lord, how he said, 'John baptized with water, but you will be baptized in the Holy Spirit.'"

So before the passion the apostles had been baptized with water and washed. But that washing was for the forgiveness of sins, not a sharing in the Holy Spirit. For it says, "John came preaching in the wilderness a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins." How shall we know that the apostles had this baptism? Let us show it. He did not say, "John baptized you with water," but simply "John baptized." That does not yet make it clear whether he baptized the apostles. So how is it clear? When Peter objected, saying, "Lord, you shall never wash my feet," the Savior said, "Unless I wash you, you have no part with me." Peter answered, "Lord, not only my feet, but also my hands and my head." The Savior answered, "One who has bathed has no need to wash, except for his feet." Do you see how he ratified that washing? Where Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have not been named, it is only a baptism of repentance; but where they have been named, it is a baptism of adoption. The Savior did not set aside the baptism of repentance but completed it, and to the baptism in the Trinity he added the gift of the Holy Spirit. But the heretics, as far as it lay with them, have set aside a baptism ratified by the Trinity. They did not respect the Master's word: "One who has bathed has no need to wash, except for his feet." "But you will be baptized in the Holy Spirit not many days from now."

Next comes the greedy, meddling curiosity of human nature. It is typical of human beings to ask: When is the consummation? When is Christ coming? How many years until the end? When will his kingdom appear? The apostles indulge this human failing and begin to question the Savior: "So when they had come together, they asked him, 'Lord, is this the time when you will restore the kingdom to Israel?'" Since he had told them, "When the Son of Man comes in his glory," they say, "Is it at this time?" They wanted to learn whether what they hoped for was near at hand, or whether salvation would be slow in coming. Then the Savior: "It is not for you to know times or seasons, which the Father has set by his own authority." The apostles were not allowed even to investigate times. Are heretics then allowed to investigate the substance that is beyond time, the eternal nature? So when a heretic argues about such things and says, "How did the Father beget? What is the manner of the divine begetting?" turn the Lord's own words back on him: "It is not for you to know times or seasons." It is not for you to know God's begetting and substance. It is not for you, and it is not for the angels either, nor the archangels, nor any created power whatever. Then whose is it to know? "No one knows the Father except the Son, nor the Son except the Father," nor "the depths of God except the Spirit of God." "It is not for you to know times or seasons." Do you not respect the limits set for the apostles? Those who were gathered together, to whom he appeared, who were enlightened by him, are not permitted to know. Instead they are taught not to overstep their limits, and they heard, "It is not for you to know times or seasons." And you go investigating? But Daniel learned times and seasons and measures: "Seventy weeks," he says, "have been decreed for your people. From the going forth of the word for the temple to be rebuilt: seven weeks and sixty-two weeks, and one." So it was possible to learn about times. But he uses the times to muzzle their boldness, so that people may learn that if they are not permitted to learn about times, they have much less business investigating the divine begetting. "It is not for you to know times or seasons, which the Father has set by his own authority." So the Son did not set them? Are ages and times in the Father's authority, and the Son has no share in them? If the Son has no share in times and seasons and ages, Paul is lying when he says, "In these last days he has spoken to us by a Son, through whom he also made the ages." If the Son is the maker of the ages, they are also in the Son's authority. And this is what Paul means: "which the Father has set by his own authority." He calls the Son the Father's authority, then, just as he calls him the Father's power and wisdom, for "Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God." "It is not for you to know times or seasons, but you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you." You will receive power, not to pry into times and seasons, but to believe in the Lord.

"And you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth." Do not measure the order of the words, but the power of the authority behind them. He said, "Preach me everywhere." This shows power, if the word turned into fact. I could take authority on myself and swagger, and say to the people around me, or to a few servants or brothers: "Go out to the nations, teach them everything, convert everyone, destroy the barbarians, cut down those who oppose my kingdom." The words go out, but if the deeds do not follow, I am condemned not only as a liar but as a braggart and a reckless man. So let the Savior's words be judged, not by what he said, but by what he accomplished. He said, "Make disciples of all nations." If the word had not become deed, it would have been bragging and not divine authority. He said, "Preach to the end of the earth." If there is any far corner of the earth with no share in the preaching, the prediction was false. But if the deeds shine out even ahead of the words, then the witnesses are true, and the one they bear witness to is true.

"And when he had said this, as they were watching, he was lifted up." "As they were watching": he could have ascended without being seen, but just as he had the disciples' eyes as witnesses of the resurrection, so he makes them eyewitnesses of the ascension as well. Luke, the writer of the gospel, added: "And having said this, he led them out as far as Bethany," to the Mount of Olives, where he had also raised Lazarus. For he was taken up from the very place where he had exercised his life-giving power. We have already said that the Savior accomplishes one thing by means of another. He chooses a place for the ascension close to where Lazarus was raised, so that the nearness of the place might remind the disciples: "Do not be amazed if he who gave life to others lives, and goes up alive." So Luke says that he led them out as far as Bethany and said to them, "Stay in the city of Jerusalem until you are clothed with power from on high."

Learn that the power is one and the same: the believer puts on Christ, and puts on the Holy Spirit. If the one is foreign to the other, how is a royal garment insulted when it is put on someone who is not a king? No one puts on a common garment over purple, for that insults the dignity of kingship. Believers, then, put on Christ: "For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ." The Holy Spirit is God, and Christ is God. How then could he say again, "Put on the Holy Spirit," unless the Spirit were God, and the Son God as well? I say this to the followers of Macedonius, who limp where the Spirit is concerned. If the Spirit is not God, if it is not divine grace, how can those who have put on Christ, a divine garment, put on a common garment over him? "For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ." "Remain in Jerusalem until you are clothed with power from on high." What power? "You will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you." A garment means a tunic. The Holy Spirit too is the believers' garment, not as a cloak is, but in the way iron puts on fire: not wrapped around it from outside, but blended into it through and through. That is how believers put on Christ: not as a cloak lying around them on the outside, but as one who fills the heart, enlightens the hearing, calms the thoughts, and fills the face with grace. For if the grace of Christ did not shine out on the outside, how could those who gazed at Stephen's face have seen his face like the face of an angel? So he says, "Stay in this city until you are clothed with power from on high, and you will be my witnesses."

Pay attention, I beg you. "And lifting up his hand, he blessed them." Do you see what the historian has pointed out? He presents the Savior blessing, but never bringing his blessings to an end. He did not say, "He blessed them and finished," but, "Lifting up his hands, he blessed them. And while he was blessing them, he was taken up." From the moment he begins to bless, he never stops blessing. "Lifting up his hands." The Savior does two things. He spreads out his hands, giving the priests a pattern, so that by spreading out their hands they may bless the people. For since it is the invisible right hand that blesses everyone, the invisible borrows the visible: the priest stretches out his hands as though lending the Lord a pen, so that he may write the blessing with it. That he wants the priests' hands to be stretched out, hear from him directly. God says to Moses: "Say to Aaron your brother: When you come out from the altar, stretch out your hands over the people and invoke my name, and I will bless them." Here he has brought down the arrogance of the proud. For sometimes many people, instead of examining their own lives, pry into the lives of others, and their minds are divided: "Am I to bow my head to this man? Am I to go to him so that he can bless me?" Then you have condemned me, but not the name. Am I the one who promises to bless, that you should run away? I invoke the name of God, and he himself blesses. If an imperial rescript is sent to you, do you scrutinize the life of the man who brought it, or the gift of the one who sent it? You do not ask what rank the emperor's messenger holds, whether he is a peasant or a townsman, a senator or an official. The rank of the messenger makes no difference; you receive the honor of the sender.

So the Savior, showing the marks, spreads out his hands and blesses at the same time. He keeps showing the marks right up to the final moment of the ascension, so that he may at once complete the blessing and display the passion: the very body that suffered, that was crucified and nailed, is what is taken up. Pay attention. The marks remained like visible scars, gleaming with brightness, and these scars will not fade away until the final coming. For just as he gave the disciples full assurance that he had died and risen, so the Jews who crucified him must also be given full assurance that the one they insulted is himself reigning, and the prophet's oracle is fulfilled: "They will look on him whom they pierced." And then all the tribes of the earth will look, of the Jews not all [?]. For the glory of the one who suffered shames those who disbelieved as much as it crowns those who believed. Have you not seen in imperial images how the ranks of the bodyguards stand by, and in what humiliation the enemies are made subject? How in the upper register the companions of the emperor's reign stand beside him with great confidence, made bold by their share in his glory, while those taken captive by the law of war lie in chains under his feet in the same image, the one group beside him, the other beneath him? So it will be when the Lord of all appears in the flesh at his second coming, and shows the marks of the nails and those wounds shining with immortality. He will set the saints beside himself, like companions of his reign, shining with royal belts and standing by the throne of the kingdom. And all who opposed the cross, Jews and Greeks, and the heretics who raged against his divinity, he will present, some as captives, others he will crucify. Have you not seen crowds of barbarians, some bound and others slaughtered? The same happens with Christ: all who speak against him will be bound, as it is written: "To bind their kings with fetters and their nobles with iron manacles, to carry out on them the judgment that is written." Then, when this has come to pass, what will follow? "This is the glory of all his holy ones." That they will be bound is clearly stated; but where is it said that they will also be slaughtered? By slaughter I mean not bloodshed, but punishment at the judgment.

Again the Scripture recalls it, saying: "A certain nobleman went to a distant country to receive a kingdom for himself." From earth to heaven. He did not say "to receive it from someone," but "for himself." "A certain nobleman went to a distant country to receive a kingdom for himself and to return." He comes with the kingdom; he came having received the kingdom for himself. "But his citizens" (the Jews) "hated him and sent an embassy, saying, 'We do not want this man to reign over us.'" Where did they send an embassy? When Pilate cried out, "Shall I crucify your king?" they said, "We have no king but Caesar," rejecting him. "After a long time had passed, that nobleman returned, holding the kingdom," and first he summoned his own servants, to whom he had entrusted the talents, and said, "How much have you gained by trading?" Whom did you help? Whom did you teach? Whom did you enlighten? The first says to him, "Lord, your mina has made ten minas" — I have multiplied the preaching tenfold, he means. And the king says to him, "Well done, good and faithful servant; you shall have authority over ten cities." Then the king appoints rulers, handing them their tablets of office. Then he says to the second, "And what did you do?" He says, "Lord, your mina has made five minas." He says to him, "You too, be over five cities." He did not say to him, "Why did you not make it tenfold as well?" Rather, he asks interest from each according to his ability. For each will receive his own reward according to his own labor. He says to the other, "And what did you do?" That one says, "Lord, here is your talent. I knew that you are a hard man, reaping what you did not sow and gathering where you did not scatter, so I tied the talent up in a cloth. Here is what is yours." And the master says, "Take the talent from him and give it to the one who has the ten talents." Then the others say, "Lord, he has ten talents." What does he answer? "Truly, truly, I tell you, to the one who has, more will be given; but from the one who does not have, even what he seems to have will be taken away." Having laid out the story in this way, he crowns his own and slaughters his enemies. David described this image of those who worship and those who fall when he said: "All the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the Lord" (those who believed), "and all the families of the nations will worship before him, for the kingdom is the Lord's." Having described the rank of those who worship, he also introduces the rank of those who fall down: "Before him all who go down to the earth will fall."

So he showed the disciples the marks of the nails. It was from this point that our discourse took this course: the marks remain until his coming, so that his own, when they see them then, may glory in having rightly believed in the Crucified, while his enemies, who opposed the Crucified, will be put to shame. Of them Paul says: "For many are going about, of whom I have often told you, the enemies of the cross of Christ, whose end is destruction."

"So while he was blessing them, he parted from them and was carried up into heaven." This is in the gospel, and the same author says in Acts: "As they were watching, he was lifted up, and a cloud took him out of their sight." From now on created nature serves him, not as human flesh, but as God. A cloud carries the Lord, so that the oracle of the prophet David may be fulfilled: "He makes the clouds his chariot." "A cloud took him out of their sight, and they were gazing into heaven as he was going." He no longer speaks of him being taken up, but of him going. For he was taken up in the form of his flesh, but he went by his own authority.

"And as they were gazing into heaven as he was going, suddenly two men in white clothing stood beside them." The angels appeared in the form of men; this happened on the Mount of Olives. Our church has been given the same name as this mount, and there too you have not lacked two men in white clothing. For there, in place of two men dressed in white, you had Saint Alcimus and Philemon, the holy martyrs, ever shining in the white garment of martyrdom. The angels said to them, "Men of Galilee." Blessed are those who are worthy of this address! Whenever the enemies of true religion reproach us, they call us Galileans. The angels honor us: "Men of Galilee." Those who do not know what our name means think they are insulting us. We who are called Galileans are those to whom revelation has been given. For Christ performed his first sign in Cana of Galilee, and there he revealed his glory. "Men of Galilee": this is why the prophet ranks Galilee above the whole earth. For Isaiah says: "The earth has mourned, Lebanon has been put to shame, Sharon has become marshland; Galilee and Carmel will be made manifest."

"Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven?" The angels do not say "why do you stand" as a reproach. For what could be more convincing than to see the Savior being taken up? But since he had said, "You will be my witnesses," the angels say: Why do you stand here idle? Remember his commands. "Why do you stand looking into heaven?" Is he coming back to you again today? "Why do you stand looking? This Jesus, who was taken up from you..." Since "taken up" was unworthy of God, they do not say, "This only-begotten Son, who was taken up." For God is not taken up, since he is in heaven and on earth and everywhere. "This Jesus": that is, this flesh of the Lord. For where Scripture indicates something bodily, it uses the demonstrative word and the name Jesus. This Jesus who was seen, what appeared from Mary. "This Jesus," just as Peter also says: "Therefore let the whole house of Israel know for certain that God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified." He does not say "this Son" or "the only-begotten," but "Jesus." For the suffering belongs to what was visible, while the divinity is beyond suffering, even though it was united with the one who suffered. I do not say that it abandoned his body when it suffered; rather, the one beyond suffering was wholly in the one who suffered, the immortal nature in the mortal.

"Why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven." Elijah had been taken up before this, but he was taken up into the height of the air, not into heaven. So that the two ascensions should not be thought equal in honor, Scripture says there "as if into heaven," but here "into heaven." "He will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven." There it says, "Elijah was taken up as if into heaven": there, by the words "as if," Scripture set a firm limit on the height. "And Elijah was taken up as if into heaven"; but this is something different. And in this way God gave the prophets full assurance that Elijah was not taken up into heaven. Indeed, they say to Elisha, since Elijah had gone up to a height but had not reached heaven: "Take fifty men and send them to all the mountains and hills; perhaps the Spirit has taken him up and set him down on one of the mountains, and we do not know where he is." Fifty were sent to search, but none of them knew for sure where to search. That is why it says, "He was taken up as if into heaven." The Jews imagine things and say that Elijah was taken up into heaven and will himself come from heaven. The Savior shows the truth from the historical record, and makes the true teaching plain from his own instruction. He proclaims the truth when he says to Nicodemus: "No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man." Enoch was transferred on high, not taken up: he was moved from one place to another, not from earth to heaven. Elijah was taken up as if into heaven. "No one has ascended into heaven except the one from heaven, who is in heaven." And Paul, ruling out all doubt, says about Christ: "What does 'he ascended' mean, except that he had first descended into the lower parts of the earth? He who descended is the same one who also ascended far above the heavens." Not only into heaven, he says, but above it. That is why the angels say: "Why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven." "Into heaven" three times, to match that other saying: "What God has made clean, you must not call common."

That he was being taken up could be seen. But how he would come — how did the angels know that? From what the Holy Spirit spoke through the prophet, and from what the Savior promised. For when Caiaphas was raging and said, "I adjure you by the living God: are you the Christ, the Son of the living God?" he answered him, "You have said it; and from now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of the Power and coming on the clouds of heaven." Since, then, he was taken up on a cloud and will come on a cloud, they say: "He will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven." And see how wonderful this is, brothers. When an emperor goes out to display his majesty, or his army, or others who celebrate an imperial festival, he does not use just one carriage; many others follow, even if they carry no one. In the same way, when Christ is about to arrive in the kingdom of his glory, it will not be one cloud carrying him; many will accompany him. For he will come on the clouds. When he was taken up, one was enough, for "a cloud took him up." When he comes, he will come with many clouds. If he comes alone, what need is there for many clouds? Pay attention, I beg you. Here below, a carriage follows the emperor carrying nothing, purely in his honor. But then many clouds will follow the Savior, so that the saints may be caught up from the earth after the resurrection and taken up in the clouds. In this way they will share in the ascension too, and having gone out to meet the king, they will come with him, not walking but seated, not as an escort on foot but themselves carried on clouds. Where do we learn this? Paul says: "For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God. And the dead in Christ will rise first; then we who are alive will be caught up in the clouds to meet the Lord." The clouds are for the apostles' sake; for himself one was enough, for the sake of bodily sight. "For we will be caught up in the clouds to meet the Lord" — like officials going out to meet the emperor — "to meet the Lord in the air; and so we will always be with the Lord." Then those left behind on the earth, humbled, unworthy of the glory, liable to punishment for their unbelief, begin to see the king and those who go out to meet him. And the saints are found to be like those arriving with him, for whoever goes out to meet the emperor and then turns back is found to be entering with him. And this comes about in fulfillment of the prophetic saying: "The Lord my God will come, and all the saints with him." So they come in clouds to meet the Lord, and they will be caught up. "So this Jesus, who was taken up from you, will come in the same way."

See how many details Scripture gives, so as to make us certain on every point: "While they were watching, he was lifted up"; "he parted from them and was carried up"; "and a cloud took him"; "and as they were gazing into heaven while he went." He was taken up, he was lifted up, he was carried up, he entered: "For Jesus did not enter a holy place made with hands, but into heaven itself, to appear before God." He did not only enter; he also passed through. "For we have," says Paul, "a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus." He went up, he ascended, he was taken up, he went on his way, he passed through. Pay attention. He ascended as one who has authority, so that the prophet's oracle might be fulfilled: "God has gone up with a shout." Here the prophet uses a plain, unadorned word: "God has gone up with a shout." "Lift up your gates, you rulers, and be lifted up, you everlasting gates, and the King of glory shall come in." He shall come in: "For Jesus did not enter a holy place made with hands, but into heaven itself"; the King of glory shall come in. So two things happened. The earth was astonished when it saw the Savior clothed in a body. It is our habit, when we see an unfamiliar face, to say, "Who is this?", for no one asks about someone he knows. In the same way the earth, seeing the Savior wielding divine power and giving orders to the winds and the sea, says, "Who is this, that even the sea and the winds obey him?" And just as the earth in its astonishment cried out, "Who is this?", so heaven, astonished to see the Godhead in flesh, says, "Who is this King of glory?"

And see the marvel. The Savior came, and when he came he brought the Holy Spirit; when he went up he took up a holy body, so that he might give the world a pledge of salvation, the Holy Spirit. And again, let the Christian say that for this same world the holy body is the guarantee of salvation. When I say this, I mean you and every single Christian. "I am a Christian; I belong to God." How so? "I have the Holy Spirit, who is from heaven." Do you want another proof? "I received the Spirit of God from heaven; I hold my guarantee." His body is above; his Spirit is below with us. Do you doubt that we belong to God? God and human beings have become one family. For just as a marriage joins parties that were apart, and when one woman and one man are united, two whole families are joined, even someone who did not know where the other came from, so that one becomes nephew and the other uncle; so too, when Christ took flesh, through that flesh the whole Church became kin to Christ: Paul is Christ's kinsman, Peter, every believer, all of us, every devout person. That is why Paul says, "Since, then, we are God's offspring." I know the sense in which that was said; my aim is not to set out the whole interpretation, only to show that Paul confirms the kinship. And elsewhere again: "We are the body of Christ, and members in part, of his flesh." That is: because of the flesh he took on, we are his kin. So we have the pledge above, and the Holy Spirit with us. And see the marvel. I do not say that the Spirit came down from heaven and is no longer in heaven, as though they had traded places, the body taking heaven and the Spirit the earth. No, the Spirit is both with us and everywhere and above: "Where shall I go from your Spirit?" And why are you amazed that the Spirit is both with us and above, and the body of Christ both above and with us? Heaven has the holy body, and earth has received the Holy Spirit; Christ came and brought the Holy Spirit, he went up and took up our body. And one could see the image of Adam, once buried in tombs, no longer appearing among angels but seated above the angels together with God, so that he might seat us with him too.

O strange dispensation! O great King! All these things belong to the Great One, the one who is truly great and wonderful. As the prophet said: "O Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is your name in all the earth, for your majesty is lifted up above the heavens!" Was the Godhead lifted up? No! God, who is in heaven and on earth, is not taken up. It was my flesh, the form of the servant, not the image of God. The very words are: "While they were watching, he was lifted up." He is great in all things: great God, great Lord. "Great is the Lord and greatly to be praised." And if he is great God and great Lord, he is a great King: "A great King over all the earth." "Mount Zion, the sides of the north, the city of the great King." Great prophet, great priest, great light, great in all things. And Scripture always calls him great with that word added, as when Paul says, "of our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ"; as David also says, "Great is the Lord and greatly to be praised." Great King, great prophet: when Jesus was working his miracles, people said, "A great prophet has arisen," and, "God has visited his people." For he is great not only in his Godhead but also in his flesh. Just as in his Godhead he is great God, great Lord and great King, so again he is great priest and great prophet. How do we know? Paul says: "Since, then, we have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast to our confession." And if he is a great high priest and a great prophet, God truly visited his people and raised up a great prophet in Israel. And if he is a great prophet and a great priest, he is also a great light: "Galilee of the Gentiles, the people who sat in darkness, saw a great light." His day, too, is great, as the prophet says: "Before the great day of the Lord comes." When you hear "great" everywhere, and "great are the works of the Lord," what put it into your head, heretic, to divide the Great One and make him small?

So we have the guarantee of our life in heaven, for we were taken up together with Christ. And we will again be caught up in the clouds, if we are worthy to go out to meet him on the clouds. A defendant does not go out to meet the judge; he appears before him, standing there, but he does not go out to meet him, because he has no confidence. Let us pray, then, that we may be among those who go out to meet him, even if in a lowly rank. For just as those who go out to meet a king are all honored, even though they are not all equal in honor, so it will be then. Not everyone has lived in the same way. Each will receive his own reward according to his own labor. Let not one word ever hinder another. For we speak boldly and truthfully, feeding the people with the love of Christ and watering their souls; we share ourselves out among souls, but we are not divided by suspicions. The enemy of peace has one who will judge him. And since, brothers, we persuade human beings but are laid open to God, the one who watches over our thoughts is my witness, he who will call to account everyone who speaks falsehood, that we have never been enemies of peace, and have never wished, nor do we wish, to become such. For if we lose peace, we are enemies of those who hear, "Peace be with you." But that we want peace, strive for it and long for it, he who knows is witness. About the rest I will keep silent. For one who awaits God as his judge does not insult the court above by making a defense. God is able to give peace and to establish peace among those who preach and those who are preached to, among those who teach and those who learn, so that, having begun from peace in all things, continued in peace and completed our course in peace, we may send up glory to the God of peace, the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
